source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Overall pooled effect of choice architecture on behaviour is small to medium, and robust to outlier removal and leave-one-out.
numbers: 455 effect sizes, 214 publications, N=2,149,683. d=0.45 (95% CI 0.39-0.52). Without influential outliers d=0.42 (0.37-0.46). Leave-one-out d 0.43-0.46. Raw d ranged -0.69 to 4.69.
limits: Unadjusted for publication bias. Many effects come from low-powered studies.
agent_relevance: Gives the naive prior for any scaffold nudge: about 0.4 SD if you believe the published record, far less if you do not. Do not budget on it.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Huge heterogeneity: most of the spread is real variation between interventions, and about 15% of interventions are expected to backfire.
numbers: I2=99.67%, tau2=0.23. 95% prediction interval for a new study [-0.48, 1.39]. About 15% of interventions predicted to reduce or reverse the target behaviour.
limits: Heterogeneity is not explained well by the coded moderators (I2 only falls to 99.52% with category x domain).
agent_relevance: A single average is a poor guide. Under G7 each scaffold change must be measured on the agent's own task; transfer from a pooled mean is unreliable.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Publication bias is detected by Egger test and funnel asymmetry. Authors say the true effect is likely smaller than their model estimate.
numbers: Egger b=2.28 (95% CI 1.31-3.25), t(339)=4.61, p<0.001. Moderate one-tailed bias cuts d from 0.42 to 0.31 (-26.79%). Severe one-tailed bias cuts it to d=0.03.
quote: the true effect size of interventions is likely to be smaller than estimated by our meta-analytic model
limits: Weight-function sensitivity analysis; authors say severe bias is only partly supported by the funnel plot. Reply letter later quotes d=0.08 for severe.
agent_relevance: Positive-result filtering inflates any improvement claim. For our loop: report all arms, including nulls, before keeping a change (G7).

source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Decision structure interventions (defaults, changing effort or option layout) beat decision information and decision assistance.
numbers: Structure d=0.55 (0.45-0.64), k=227, n=357,179. Information d=0.38 (0.29-0.47), k=130. Assistance d=0.31 (0.23-0.39), k=98. Category F(3,337)=9.79. Structure vs information b=0.17, vs assistance b=0.24. Nine techniques each d 0.30-0.62.
limits: Maier et al. find structure the only category not ruled out after bias correction, but its interval is wide.
agent_relevance: Changing the environment the agent acts in (what is shown first, what is default) may matter more than telling it what to do. Supports structural scaffolds over added instructions, but test it.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Domain moderates the effect. Food is largest, finance smallest.
numbers: Food d=0.72 (0.49-0.95). Finance d=0.25 (0.12-0.37). Domain F(6,334)=4.62. Abstract: food up to 2.5 times larger than other domains.
limits: Food stays indecisive but not clearly null after bias correction (Maier et al.).
agent_relevance: Effect depends on task family. Do not pool scaffold results across task types.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Setting (lab vs natural field), location (US vs elsewhere) and age group did not moderate the effect. Newer publications report smaller effects.
numbers: Only publication year predicted effect size (smaller in recent years). No difference between lab, artifactual, framed and natural field experiments.
limits: A decline with year fits early small-n positive results followed by larger trials.
agent_relevance: A shrinking effect over time in a literature is a warning sign for any early large gain in our own loop; re-measure.

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
finding: Re-analysis of the Mertens data with robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA PSMA: selection models plus PET-PEESE) finds the overall effect near zero once bias is modelled.
numbers: Random effects d=0.43 [0.38,0.48]. RoBMA PSMA d=0.04 [0.00,0.14], BF01=0.95 (undecided). Using only the most precise estimate per study: d=0.11 [0.00,0.24], BF01=0.31 (weak evidence for an effect). Reported Egger b=2.10.
quote: when this publication bias is appropriately corrected for, no evidence for the effectiveness of nudges remains
limits: Authors admit the three-level structure cannot be modelled with bias correction; two workarounds. Letter, not full paper. Heterogeneity remains, so some nudges can still work.
agent_relevance: Headline for our G7: published gains can vanish under bias correction. Keep a no-change control and pre-register what counts as improvement.

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
finding: By category after bias correction: information and assistance nudges show evidence against an effect; structure is undecided.
limits: Structure estimate has a wide interval; evidence is undecided, not for absence.
agent_relevance: Reminders and added information are the weakest class. Prompt-text tips in a scaffold are likely the same class; structural changes are the better bet.

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
finding: By domain after bias correction: finance has strong evidence of no effect; food, prosocial and other stay undecided.
numbers: Finance raw 0.23 -> RoBMA 0.00, BF01=41.23 (precise 30.95). Health raw 0.31 -> 0.01, BF01=8.98. Food raw 0.66 -> 0.02 [-0.09,0.32], BF01=5.16; precise 0.27, BF01=0.55 (indecisive). Environment raw 0.48 -> 0.01, BF01=4.41. Strong publication bias in all subsets (BF_pb>10) except food with precise estimates (BF_pb=2.49).
limits: Bayes factors depend on prior choices in RoBMA; subsets lose power.
agent_relevance: Even the biggest domain effect (food, up to 2.5x) is not secure. Treat the 2.5x headline as unreliable.

source: Szaszi et al. (2022) No reason to expect large and consistent effects of nudge interventions
finding: Three other bias corrections on the same Mertens data give near-zero averages. Authors see no reason to expect large and consistent effects, except for defaults.
numbers: Andrews-Kasy d=-0.01 (SE 0.02). WAAP (adequately powered studies) d=0.07 (SE 0.03). Trim and fill d=0.08 (SE 0.03). Mertens own adjusted range d=0.08 (severe) to 0.31 (moderate). Under severe bias, 95% of study effects lie within +/-1.00 of d=0.08.
quote: we see no reason to expect large and consistent effects when designing nudge experiments or running interventions
limits: Letter. Correction methods are known to be unstable under high heterogeneity.
agent_relevance: Convergence of four correction methods makes the bias worry hard to dismiss. Agree on a mechanism before adopting any nudge-like prompt trick.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) Reply to Maier, Szaszi, and Bakdash and Marusich
finding: Authors concede publication bias and heterogeneity are the two main problems and say their work was not the final word. They stand by d=0.43 as the unadjusted value and call for powered, preregistered studies.
numbers: Egger b=2.10, 95% CI [1.31,2.89], t(332)=5.22. Sensitivity attenuation to d=0.31 (moderate bias) and d=0.08 (severe bias). Unadjusted d=0.43 matches other reviews: Benartzi 2017, Beshears and Kosowsky 2020, Hummel and Maedche 2019, Jachimowicz 2019 (as cited by them).
limits: Reply letter; no new analysis.
agent_relevance: The original authors agree the corrected effect is smaller. The dispute is how much smaller, not whether.

source: DellaVigna and Linos (2020/2022) RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units
finding: At-scale nudge-unit trials give an average effect about one sixth of published academic nudge trials.
numbers: Nudge Units (Office of Evaluation Sciences, BIT North America): 126 RCTs, 243 nudges, 23.5 million people; effect 1.4 pp (SE 0.3), 8.1% over control take-up of 17.2%. Academic journals: 26 papers, 74 nudges; effect 8.7 pp (SE 2.5), 33.5% over control 26.0%.
limits: Outcome is take-up in government communications; nudge-unit trials are not exact replications of the academic ones. Published as Econometrica 2022 (NBER working paper read).
agent_relevance: Real-world scale cuts effect sizes sixfold. Expect a small-benchmark gain from a scaffold to shrink on a larger, broader task set.

source: DellaVigna and Linos (2020/2022) RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units
finding: Statistical power plus selective publication explain the whole gap.
numbers: Median treatment arm n: 484 (academic) vs 10,006 (nudge units). Minimum detectable effect at 80% power: 6.3 pp vs 0.8 pp. Academic sample has over 4 times as many studies with t in 1.96-2.96 as in 0.96-1.96; nudge units show no discontinuity. Controlling for MDE, well-powered academic nudges give about 1 pp. Selection-corrected academic mean 3.2 pp (SE 1.9) vs 8.6 uncorrected; probability a non-significant trial is published 0.1 (SE 0.1).
limits: Andrews-Kasy style model generalised to a mixture of normals; the corrected estimate is imprecise (SE 1.9).
agent_relevance: Sample size is the cheapest guard against false gains (G7): the loop should power its comparisons, not run a few items.

source: DellaVigna and Linos (2020/2022) RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units
finding: Academic involvement does not explain the gap; features of the nudge explain about two thirds of it.
numbers: BIT NA (no academics) 1.7 pp (SE 0.5). OES 1.0 pp (SE 0.2); OES with academics 1.0 pp (SE 0.4). Controlling for medium (in-person vs letter) and mechanism, without power, explains two thirds of the gap.
limits: Features are correlated with power (in-person nudges run with small samples).
agent_relevance: Delivery form matters more than who designs it. Fits the idea that structure and channel dominate wording.

source: DellaVigna and Linos (2020/2022) RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units
finding: Experts overpredict nudge-unit effects; practitioners are almost calibrated.
numbers: Median forecast of academic-sample effect 6 pp (mean 8 pp). Median forecast for nudge-unit effect 4 pp (mean 5.8 pp) vs true 1.4 pp. Practitioners median 1.95 pp.
limits: Forecaster sample sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Humans and likely LLM judges overrate gains from known tricks. Do not let the agent score its own scaffold ideas; measure.

source: Madrian and Shea (2001) The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation and Savings Behavior
finding: Founding field result: switching a large US firm to automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation sharply, with no change in economic terms.
numbers: Participation of employees hired under automatic enrollment about 86%; employees hired just before (WINDOW cohort) about half. Firm-wide participation before the change 61%, so implied steady-state rise about 25 pp. Default was 3% contribution into a money market fund.
limits: One firm, cohort comparison (not randomised), 78% female workforce, short tenure window.
agent_relevance: A default that sets the agent's starting point can dominate later reasoning. Check which default the scaffold implicitly sets.

source: Madrian and Shea (2001) The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation and Savings Behavior
finding: The default also anchors contribution rate and fund, a side effect that hurts savings.
numbers: 65.1% of the auto-enrolled cohort contribute exactly 3%; 12.2 pp above what would be predicted if all new participants chose 3%. Full default pattern (participate, 3%, money market) 61% for the new cohort vs 1% for other cohorts. New cohort puts 80% of contributions in money market and 16% in stocks; other cohorts about 70% in stocks and under 10% in money market.
limits: Observational; some employees may have chosen the default for good reasons.
agent_relevance: A nudge can pull people to a worse point than they would have chosen on a dimension not targeted. Measure side effects, not just the target.

source: Johnson and Goldstein (2003) Do Defaults Save Lives? Science 302
finding: Online experiment and cross-country data on organ donation defaults: opt-out wording roughly doubles stated consent versus opt-in.
numbers: Online experiment, 161 respondents: consent 42% opt-in, 82% opt-out, 79% neutral (values read from the figure). Cross-country effective consent: explicit-consent countries 4.25% (Denmark), 12% (Germany), 17.17% (Netherlands), 27.5% (UK); presumed-consent countries mostly 85.9% to 99.98%.
limits: Effective consent is registration, not actual donation. Cross-country data confound culture, law and infrastructure. Later work (not read) reports much smaller actual donation differences.
agent_relevance: The paper lists three mechanisms: implied endorsement, effort, loss aversion. The implied-endorsement route matches how LLMs read suggestions.

source: Johnson and Goldstein (2003) Do Defaults Save Lives? Science 302
finding: Panel check: donation rose after countries adopted presumed consent.
numbers: Presumed consent raised donation by 16.3% (p<0.02), 14.1 to 16.4 million (panel by year). Using a 1999 cross-section of more countries (Gimbel et al.), 10.8 to 16.9, a 56.5% increase.
limits: Not randomised; confounds acknowledged in text.
agent_relevance: Even the founding effect mixes mechanism and measurement choices; confirm outcomes are actual behaviour.

source: Milkman et al. (2021) A megastudy of text-based nudges encouraging patients to get vaccinated at an upcoming doctor's appointment (PNAS)
finding: Megastudy of 19 text messages by 26 scientists, 47,306 patients, preregistered: small gains, many nudges null, true effects not distinguishable from each other.
numbers: Control vaccination 42%. 6 of 19 messages significant (32%); all 19 directionally positive. Average +2.1 pp (5%), p=0.024. Best message +4.6 pp (11%); shrunk estimate for winner's curse +2.8 pp (6.7%). Cannot reject equal true effects, chi2=21.277, df=18, p=0.266.
limits: Flu shots only, US health systems, text reminders (a weak, assistance-type nudge).
agent_relevance: Picking the best of many prompt variants overstates its gain (winner's curse). In our loop: re-run the winner on fresh items before keeping it (G7).

source: Milkman et al. (2021) Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science (Nature 600)
finding: Gym megastudy: 54 four-week programmes designed by 30 scientists, 61,293 gym members; judges could not predict the winners.
numbers: 45% of interventions significantly increased weekly gym visits by 9% to 27%. Only 8% showed a significant effect after the 4 weeks ended. Best: micro-rewards for returning after a missed workout. (Abstract only read.)
limits: Abstract-level evidence; full text did not load.
agent_relevance: Forecasts by judges failed: confirms why measured comparison, not intuition, picks scaffold variants.

source: Milkman et al. (2025) Can reminder emails compel Americans to save? A two-million-person megastudy
finding: Nearly 2 million bank customers, seven email nudge campaigns: effects are tiny.
numbers: Average +0.05 pp in one-time savings deposit probability (0.51% over control). Best campaign +0.13 pp (1.32%). Estimated extra savings USD 6.1 to 9.9 million across the population. (Abstract only read.)
limits: Abstract-level evidence. Light-touch email, one bank.
agent_relevance: At very large N the same nudge gives real but minuscule effects. Matches DellaVigna and Linos: small and cheap.

source: Bryan, Tipton, Yeager (2021) Behavioural science is unlikely to change the world without a heterogeneity revolution
finding: Argues that failed replications mostly reflect real heterogeneity of effects across people and contexts, so the field needs systematic sampling and moderator study.
numbers: No effect numbers in the abstract. (Abstract only read.)
limits: Position paper; abstract only.
agent_relevance: The unit of evidence should be which task type and which model, not whether scaffold X works.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2026) AI agents are sensitive to nudges. PNAS
finding: Fourteen frontier LLMs vs humans on a multiattribute sequential choice task with defaults, suggestions, highlighting and resource-rational optimal nudges. Most LLMs are hypersensitive to defaults.
numbers: Human: default basket chosen 51% in control, 88% with default. LLMs with default: GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-5 Mini 99%; Gemini 1.5 Flash 94%; GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Claude 3 Haiku, o3 Mini 100%. Not different from humans: Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, o3, GPT-5.
limits: Stylised cost-of-information task; prompts base, chain-of-thought and few-shot human data. Some models were inversely hypersensitive.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G7: weaker models follow any default near-deterministically, so a default in our scaffold would strongly steer them. Stronger reasoning models behave human-like.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2026) AI agents are sensitive to nudges. PNAS
finding: Suggestions and highlighting: models overshoot, even when the cue is uninformative or only its timing differs.
numbers: Early random suggestion accepted by humans 35%, late 25%. Many models exceed this: late-suggestion acceptance 42-77%; Gemini 2.5 Flash 13% and o3 Mini 7% fell below humans. First reveal from highlighted row when the highlight is wrong: humans 57%; Gemini 1.5 Pro 100%, Gemini 1.5 Flash 98%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 97%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 91%, GPT-5 Mini 95%. o3, GPT-5, Claude 4.5 Sonnet like humans.
limits: Same limits as above; reasoning models cost more tokens.
agent_relevance: Cues are followed even when wrong. An agent should treat any scaffold-supplied hint as evidence to check, not a command.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2026) AI agents are sensitive to nudges. PNAS
finding: A resource-rational optimal nudge (pre-revealing the most informative cells) raises payoffs for humans and for many models; some models ignore information value.
numbers: Points earned with random, extreme, optimal pre-reveals: humans 163, 170, 175; GPT-5 172, 177, 180; o3 170, 174, 178; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 157, 162, 176; Claude 3 Haiku 149, 152, 161; GPT-4o Mini stuck near 130-138. Information-search distributions differ from humans for nearly all models (KS D=0.27 to 0.98).
limits: Optimal nudge derived from a human cognitive model (Callaway, Hardy, Griffiths); transfer to LLMs only partial.
agent_relevance: A model-based nudge that supplies the most informative item first is a testable scaffold operator with a clear payoff curve.

source: Cherep et al. (2026) A framework for studying AI agent behavior: evidence from consumer choice experiments (ABxLab, ICLR 2026)
finding: 17 LLMs in a web shopping environment: ratings, prices, order and persuasive text each move choice far more than for humans.
numbers: 80,000+ trials, 17 models. Higher rating raises selection by 30-80 pp for 14 of 17 models (o4 Mini +81.2 pp; GPT-4o Mini still +20 pp, four times human). Price: 13 of 17 prefer cheaper, 15.2 pp (o3) to 34.3 pp (GPT-4o Mini); Llama 4 Maverick +93.2 pp when ratings matched. Order: GPT-4.1 Nano +90 pp for the first item, Claude 3.5 Haiku -35.4 pp. Best seller or Buy 1 Get 1 Free text shifts choice 10-60 pp in 14 of 17 models (Claude Sonnet 4 +55.9 pp, GPT-4o +62.1 pp).
limits: Stated user preferences in the prompt dominate once declared; simulated shop, not live money.
agent_relevance: Position and cue effects in LLMs are huge and model-specific. Randomise order and measure sensitivity before trusting any scaffold gain.

source: Cheung, Maier, Lieder (2025) Large language models show amplified cognitive biases in moral decision-making. PNAS
finding: LLMs show stronger omission bias than humans and a no bias that flips the answer with question wording (a framing-like effect); biases arise from chatbot fine-tuning.
numbers: Study 1: 22 dilemmas vs US sample N=285. Study 2 preregistered N=474. Study 3 N=491 (Reddit dilemmas). Study 4: bias linked to fine-tuning. (Abstract only read.)
limits: Abstract only. Moral choice, not nudges proper.
agent_relevance: Wording of the question flips outputs. Mask or randomise wording in the loop (S1).

source: Askari et al. (2024) Incentivizing news consumption on social media platforms using large language models and realistic bot accounts. PNAS Nexus
finding: LLM-written bot replies used as a nudge on real users: results small and confined to already interested users.
numbers: Field experiment, 28,457 Twitter users, 28 GPT-2 bots, 2 weeks. Treated users followed more news accounts; female-bot arm liked more news. Effects small; null for political content. (Abstract only read.)
limits: Abstract only. GPT-2 is old.
agent_relevance: LLMs used as nudgers get the same small effects as human nudge units.

source: Peng et al. (2026) Digital twins are funhouse mirrors: five systematic distortions. Science Advances
finding: LLM digital twins of people are poor stand-ins; they are hyper-rational and stereotyped.
numbers: 19 preregistered studies, 164 outcomes. Average correlation with human answers r=0.20. Five distortions including hyper-rationality. (Abstract only read.)
limits: Abstract only. Not a nudge test.
agent_relevance: Do not use LLM simulated humans to estimate nudge effects: they would likely distort the size.

source: Hegde et al. (2024) Infusing behavior science into large language models for activity coaching. PLOS Digital Health
finding: Uses the COM-B behaviour-change framework inside an LLM coach via exemplar priming and re-ranking; raters score empathy and actionability higher.
numbers: 8 human raters; significant uplift in empathy and actionability for primed and re-ranked responses (no effect sizes in the abstract).
limits: Proof of concept; simulated conversations; no behaviour outcome.
agent_relevance: LLM-as-nudge-designer is validated only by rater scores, not behaviour change.
